title: Autism: understanding needs and finding useful support
intro: Autism is a lifelong difference in development that can affect communication, social interaction, sensory experience and patterns of interests or activity. Autistic people vary greatly in abilities and support needs. Some need extensive daily assistance; others live independently but face significant hidden difficulties. Good support starts with the person's own experience and goals rather than assuming that everyone with the same diagnosis needs the same approach.

sections.heading: Recognise a pattern without relying on stereotypes
paragraphs: Differences may include interpreting conversation literally, finding changes difficult, strong focused interests or being overwhelmed by sound, light or touch. Language ability and intellectual ability vary and are not interchangeable. Someone who speaks fluently can still struggle with everyday demands. Signs begin during development, but may be recognised much later, especially when coping strategies conceal difficulties. A single trait, shyness or an online score cannot establish autism. Autism is not caused by poor parenting or vaccination.

sections.heading: Ask for assessment and describe everyday functioning
paragraphs: An assessment explores developmental history, communication, behaviour and current needs, with information from the person and, where appropriate, others who know them. Explain strengths, difficulties and the effort involved in coping at school, work or home. Ask for accessible communication and sensory adjustments during appointments. Assessment also considers other explanations and coexisting conditions such as ADHD, anxiety or learning difficulties. There is no single blood test that diagnoses autism. Support for an identified need can begin while assessment is being arranged.

sections.heading: Make communication and surroundings more accessible
paragraphs: Ask what helps rather than assuming: clear language, written information, extra processing time, pictures or an alternative communication method may be useful. Explain changes in advance where possible and offer a quieter space or breaks from overwhelming environments. Do not require eye contact as proof that someone is listening. Include the person in decisions using communication they understand. Predictability and practical adjustments can reduce distress, but routines should support participation and choice rather than become rigid demands imposed by others.

sections.heading: Address distress and health needs separately
paragraphs: A sudden change in behaviour may reflect pain, illness, poor sleep, overload or an unsafe situation; do not attribute everything to autism. People who communicate without speech also need assessment and ways to express discomfort. Seek help for significant anxiety, depression, seizures, feeding problems or loss of functioning. Support or therapy should have clear, meaningful goals and be reviewed for benefit and distress. Medicines may treat particular associated symptoms or conditions, but do not cure autism. Avoid unproven cures and potentially harmful restrictive treatments.

sections.heading: Plan support across changing stages of life
paragraphs: School transitions, employment, relationships or a move can change support needs. Discuss educational adjustments, daily living skills, workplace communication and access to healthcare according to the person's priorities. Families and carers may need their own practical support and respite; this should not erase the autistic person's voice. Ask how services transfer between childhood and adulthood and who coordinates care. Review what improves wellbeing and participation, not simply what makes a person appear less autistic to others.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: an overwhelming appointment
examples.text: An autistic adult struggles to speak in a noisy waiting room. Before the next visit, the clinic offers a quieter waiting option and written questions. The patient explains their concerns more comfortably without being required to make eye contact.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: a sudden behaviour change
examples.text: A child who uses pictures to communicate suddenly stops eating and becomes distressed. The family seeks a health assessment and helps the child indicate pain, rather than treating the change as disobedience or assuming it is simply autism.

questions: What assessment and coexisting health checks are appropriate for this person's needs?
Which communication and sensory adjustments can we try now?
What goals will support wellbeing and participation, and how will we review whether the support helps?
